title: Land, food and bioenergy
summary: Land is shared among crops, pasture, forest and energy crops by a logit on profit per hectare. See why bioenergy demand raises food prices and how a carbon price can grow forests.
outcomes: You can compute profit per hectare and logit land shares
You can estimate the land needed for a bioenergy target
You can describe GCAM's land nest and its geographic land units
You can explain how land carbon is priced and how land-use emissions arise
narration_en: Every hectare of land can only do one job at a time: grow wheat, feed cattle, carry a forest, or grow grass for bioenergy. GCAM divides land among these uses according to how profitable each one is, using a logit, the same family of formulas used for energy technologies but now with a positive exponent on profit. Land is resolved by geographic land units, the overlap of thirty-two regions and river basins, and arranged in a nest, so close substitutes like different crops compete more strongly than cropland and forest. When the energy system wants more bioenergy, the price of energy grass rises, its profit per hectare rises, and land shifts toward it, which pushes up food prices. A carbon price can also be applied to land as a subsidy for holding carbon, which makes forests more profitable and can expand them. In this module you will compute profits and land shares by hand, estimate how many million hectares a bioenergy target needs, and see how yield changes the answer.
narration_ar: لا يمكن لكل هكتار من الأرض أن يؤدي إلا وظيفة واحدة في الوقت نفسه: زراعة القمح، أو تغذية الماشية، أو حمل غابة، أو زراعة العشب للطاقة الحيوية. يقسم نموذج GCAM الأرض بين هذه الاستخدامات بحسب ربحية كل منها، مستخدمًا دالة لوجيت، من العائلة نفسها المستخدمة لتقنيات الطاقة لكن بأُس موجب على الربح. وتُمثَّل الأرض بوحدات أرضية جغرافية، هي تقاطع المناطق الاثنتين والثلاثين مع أحواض الأنهار، وتُرتَّب في شجرة متداخلة، بحيث تتنافس البدائل القريبة مثل المحاصيل المختلفة بقوة أكبر من تنافس الأراضي الزراعية والغابات. وعندما يريد نظام الطاقة مزيدًا من الطاقة الحيوية يرتفع سعر عشب الطاقة، فيرتفع ربحه لكل هكتار، وتنتقل الأرض نحوه، مما يرفع أسعار الغذاء. ويمكن أيضًا تطبيق سعر الكربون على الأرض كإعانة مقابل الاحتفاظ بالكربون، مما يجعل الغابات أكثر ربحية وقد يوسّعها. في هذه الوحدة ستحسب الأرباح وحصص الأرض يدويًا، وتقدّر كم مليون هكتار يحتاجه هدف للطاقة الحيوية، وترى كيف تغيّر الإنتاجية الجواب.

diagram.title: Land competition and its links
diagram.caption: Profit per hectare sets land shares; bioenergy demand and carbon prices change profits, and land change releases or stores carbon.

nodes.label: Crop and biomass prices
nodes.detail: Crop prices clear food markets; the biomass price clears the bioenergy market that the energy system demands from (supply_land.html).

nodes.label: Profit per hectare
nodes.detail: Profit rate = (price + subsidy − variable cost − input costs) × yield, in 1975$ per area; input costs include fertiliser and water (supply_land.html).

nodes.label: Carbon price on land
nodes.detail: Landowners receive carbon price × carbon density (discounted, annualised): forests gain relative to cropland (land.html).

nodes.label: Land nest (logit)
nodes.detail: Shares by profit with exponent ρ > 0; tighter substitution inside nests than across them. Calibrated profit scalers λ reproduce base-year land (land.html).

nodes.label: Cropland and food
nodes.detail: Every crop splits into irrigated/rainfed × high/low management, allowing price-induced intensification.

nodes.label: Energy crops
nodes.detail: Dedicated energy grass enters the cropland nest; woody biomass sits in the forest nest (details_land.html).

nodes.label: Forest and natural land
nodes.detail: Forests grow back slowly: uptake follows a sigmoid with mature age of about 30–100 years (land.html).

nodes.label: Land-use change CO₂
nodes.detail: E_t = A_t·D_t − A_t−1·D_t−1 for vegetation and soil. Releases are immediate; regrowth uptake is slow (land.html).

tour.text: Prices from food and bioenergy markets set each land use's profit per hectare.
A logit on profit shares the land: more profitable uses expand, but not all at once.
Energy grass and food crops compete in the same cropland nest: bioenergy demand raises food prices.
A carbon price on land pays for stored carbon, so forests become more profitable and can expand.
Every change in land cover changes carbon stocks: clearing releases CO₂ fast, regrowth takes it back slowly.
Biomass supply feeds back to the bioenergy market, closing the energy–land loop.

sections.heading: What this component represents
sections.html: The agriculture and land use module (AgLU) decides how land is used, what crops and livestock are produced, and how much carbon land stores. Land is resolved by water-basin-based geographic land units: the overview text says more than 300, its table 396 land subregions (overview.html). Every crop is split into irrigated/rainfed × high/low management, so production can intensify when prices rise.

sections.heading: Profit and land shares
sections.html:
π = (price − cost) × yield
si = (λi πi)ρ / Σj (λj πj)ρ, ai = aparent · si

Worked example (exponent 1, equal scalers): wheat sells at $200/t, costs $120/t, yields 3 t/ha → profit (200 − 120) × 3 = $240/ha. Energy grass at $60/t, cost $30/t, 10 t/ha → (60 − 30) × 10 = $300/ha. Shares: 240 / 540 = 44% wheat, 300 / 540 = 56% grass. At a grass price of $40/t grass gets 29%; at $90/t, 71% (land.html).

sections.heading: How much land does bioenergy need?
sections.html:
land (ha) = energy (GJ) / (yield (t/ha) × energy content (GJ/t))

With 18 GJ per tonne: 10 EJ at 10 t/ha needs 10×109 / 180 = 55.6 million ha; 100 EJ needs 555.6 million ha; halve the yield and it doubles to 1,111 million ha. World cropland is roughly 1.5 billion ha, so large bioenergy targets compete seriously with food. GCAM includes default limits: a negative-emissions budget capped at a share of GDP and a biomass externality cost curve (policies.html).

sections.heading: Land carbon and land-use change emissions
sections.html:
Vegetation and soil carbon densities by land unit come from the moirai data system. Land-use change emissions are

Et = At · Dt − At−1 · Dt−1

computed separately for vegetation and soil. Clearing releases carbon immediately; regrowth follows a slow sigmoid with forest mature ages of about 30 to 100 years. A carbon price on land works as a subsidy for holding carbon stock: carbon price × carbon density × discounting and annualisation (land.html).

sections.heading: Calibration and yields
sections.html: Profit scalers λ are calibrated by inverting the share equation with base-year land shares, then carried forward. Future yields grow by agricultural productivity growth from FAO projections, scaled by SSP (+50% in SSP1/5, −50% in SSP3) (supply_land.html, ssp.html). Numeric land logit exponents are not on the doc pages; they are in the input files.

callouts.title: A useful mental model
callouts.html: Think of plots on a market street. Each landowner rents to whoever pays most per hectare, but habits, soils and contracts mean some keep their old tenants. The logit is the street's average behaviour.

callouts.title: In GCAM
callouts.html: Query aggregated land allocation and LUC emissions by region; net CO₂ = CO₂ emissions by region + LUC emissions (outputs_emissions.html). Carbon state is set by aglu.CARBON_STATE in gcamdata's constants; maps by basin with rmap::mapGCAMLand.

callouts.title: "Bioenergy is carbon-free, so more is always better"
callouts.html: Land conversion can release large stocks of carbon immediately, while regrowth takes decades, and energy crops displace food. GCAM accounts for both through land competition and LUC emissions.

callouts.title: Docs disagree
callouts.html: Protected land: the policies page says 90% of non-commercial ecosystems by default; the land page describes a suitability × IUCN method. The land page reads as the newer method. Check your release's input files.

takeaways: Land is shared among uses by a logit on profit per hectare, inside a nest
Bioenergy and food compete for cropland, so bioenergy demand can raise food prices
Land needed = energy ÷ (yield × energy content): yield matters as much as the target
Land-use change emits carbon fast and regrowth absorbs it slowly
A carbon price on land pays for stored carbon and can expand forests
